enonce_complet: ## Capture 01 — empreinte `39d422996def…` — page 1 / 10 de la visionneuse (page imprimée non visible ; haut de page coupé : titre, auteurs et affiliations hors champ) ABSTRACT Scientific progress hinges on the interplay between collective intelligence and transformative paradigm shifts, yet predicting these revolutionary events remains a persistent challenge. This study introduces a novel human-aware AI framework that integrates the evolution of knowledge structures with the social dynamics of scientific communities to forecast groundbreaking innovations. Leveraging graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs), we construct a hybrid higher-order network that unifies a domain knowledge graph—derived from millions of scientific publications—with a scientist collaboration-competition space, capturing both cooperative and competitive interactions among researchers. This approach quantifies collective intelligence by generating embeddings that reflect the intricate relationships between knowledge content and human agency. By analyzing thematic knowledge distances and social proximities within this integrated network, we identify pairs of scientific domains poised for disruptive convergence. Dynamic analysis of these embeddings further enables temporally precise predictions of paradigm shifts. Applied to the life sciences, our framework successfully aligns with historical milestones, such as Nobel Prize-winning discoveries, demonstrating its predictive power. This work offers a scalable, interpretable tool for anticipating scientific revolutions, bridging the gap between knowledge evolution and social dynamics, and providing actionable insights for fostering innovation across disciplines. KEYWORDS Collective intelligence, paradigm shifts, graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs), collaboration-competition space, human-aware AI INTRODUCTION [début de phrase hors champ] punctuated by rare, transformative paradigm shifts that redefine our understanding of the natural world (Duan et al., 2025; Fortunato et al., 2018; Hill & Stein, 2025a, 2025b; Krieger et al., 2024; Wang & Barabási, 2021; Yang et al., 2025). Collective intelligence, the enhanced problem-solving capacity emerging from group interactions, underpins the steady growth of knowledge through collaboration, peer review, and resource sharing within scientific communities (Belikov et al., 2022; Evans & Foster, 2011; Kang et al., 2025; Sourati & Evans, 2023). While the former ensures incremental progress, the latter drives exponential leaps, often with profound societal impact. Yet, despite their significance, predicting these disruptive events remains an elusive goal, hampered by the complexity of integrating the evolution of scientific knowledge with the human dynamics that catalyze innovation. The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed the landscape of scientific discovery, enabling the analysis of vast datasets to uncover hidden patterns and accelerate research across domains such as drug discovery, materials science, and climate modeling (Gao & Wang, 2024; Sourati & Evans, 2023; Wang et al., 2023). Recent advances in graph-based AI, particularly graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs), have proven adept at modeling relational systems inherent in scientific data, such as citation networks and knowledge graphs. Simultaneously, the availability of large-scale bibliographic repositories, like PubMed and OpenAlex, offers unprecedented opportunities to map the knowledge space comprehensively. However, current AI-driven approaches predominantly treat scientific literature as an abstract entity, focusing either on knowledge evolution through bibliometric trends or on collaboration networks in isolation (Franzoni & Stephan, 2023; Ghosal et al., 2022; Hoppe et al., 2023; Kumari et al., 2022). This siloed perspective overlooks a critical reality: scientific breakthroughs emerge not merely from ideas but from the interplay of those ideas with the social fabric of the researchers who develop and debate them. A growing body of evidence suggests that social proximity among scientists—whether through collaboration or competition—can amplify the potential for disruptive innovation, particularly when bridging distant knowledge domains (Lin et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2024; Yang, Ding, et al., 2024; Yang, Xu, et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2022). Yet, few frameworks effectively unify these dimensions into a predictive model capable of anticipating paradigm shifts. Traditional scientometric methods, while adept at tracking emerging trends or mapping collaboration networks, rarely connect these insights to the likelihood of transformative outcomes.

The weight of this edge, w(s_i, s_j), is quantified by the total number of joint publications between s_i and s_j, reflecting the strength of their collaborative relationship. Competition: In the absence of direct collaboration, we infer potential competition between scientists whose research exhibits significant overlap in terms of knowledge entities. Specifically, if papers authored by s_i (set P_i) and s_j (set P_j) share identical knowledge entities or contain entities that are directly connected within the domain knowledge graph, we quantify the intensity of this research overlap, c(s_i, s_j), based on the connection density within G_K: c(s_i, s_j) = |{(u,v) ∈ E_K | u ∈ P_i, v ∈ P_j}| / (|P_i| · |P_j|). Here, |{(u, v) ∈ E_K | u ∈ P_i, v ∈ P_j}| represents the total number of edges in the knowledge graph G_K that connect any paper u authored by s_i to any paper v authored by s_j, and |P_i| · |P_j| represents the total number of possible paper pairs between the two scientists. A higher value of c(s_i, s_j) suggests a greater degree of research overlap and, consequently, a higher potential for intellectual competition.
